Cu-Catalyzed C −H Allylation of Benzimidazoles with Allenes
Yaxi Dong and Bernhard Breit *
Cite This: Org. Lett. 2021, 23, 6765 −6769 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: CuH-catalyzed intramolecular cyclization and inter-
molecular allylation of benzimidazoles with allenes have been
described. The reaction proceeded smoothly with the catalytic
system of Cu(OAc)
2/Xantphos and catalytic amount of
(MeO)2MeSiH. This protocol features mild reaction conditions
and a good tolerance of substrates bearing electron-withdrawing,
electron-donating, or electron-neutral groups. A new catalytic
mechanism was proposed for this copper hydride catalytic system.
F
unctionalization of benzimidazoles is an important topic
because these sca ﬀolds widely occur in pharmaceuticals,
natural products, and functional materials. 1 For quite a long
time, the functionalization of benzimidazoles has been
enriched by classical metalation with strong bases.
2 However,
these traditional synthetic methods su ﬀer general limitations,
such as harsh reaction conditions, low chemo- and/or
regioselectivity, and poor reactivity of electron-de ﬁcient
benzimidazoles. In recent decades, direct transition-metal-
catalyzed C−H functionalization has been an e ﬀective tool for
the synthesis of benzimidazole frameworks. For examples, in
2001, Bergman and Ellman reported a Rh-catalyzed intra-
molecular cyclization of benzimidazles.
3 Cavell, Ye, and
Ackermann independently described the intramolecular
cyclization of benzimidazoles using nickel catalysts. 4 On the
other hand, there are some reported examples of intermo-
lecular C −H functionalization of benzimidazoles that rely on
alkylation, alkenylation, or alkynylation of benzimidazoles
using rhodium, palladium, or nickel catalysts.
5−7 However,
these methods still have many challenges, such as the need of a
strong base, high temperature, and limited scope of
benzimidazoles. Therefore, the development of e ﬀective
synthetic methodologies is undoubtedly urgent and challeng-
ing.
In the past few years, CuH catalysis has been widely applied
to the hydrofunctionalization of alkenes, alkynes, and ketones
with various electrophiles. 8 However, only a few electron-
deﬁcient heterocycles have been studied. For examples,
Buchwald and Ge independently reported several examples
of CuH-catalyzed C −H alkylation of N-heterocycles, e.g.,
pyridines, indazoles, and quinolines. 9 Recently, Buchwald and
co-workers described a CuH-ca talyzed branch-selective
alkylation of benzimidazoles with 1,3-dienes ( Scheme 1 a).10
Xu and co-workers developed a CuH-catalyzed branch-
selective alkylation of benzimidazoles with alkenes ( Scheme
1b).11 The typical CuH catalytic process undergoes a
hydrocupration of alkene followed by the addition to the
CN bond and regeneration of CuH species with an over-
stoichiometric amount of hydrosilane. Our group has
described a Rh- and Pd-catalyzed regiodivergent and stereo-
selective N allylation of imidazoles with allenes.
12 In line with
our continued interest in functionalization of benzimidazoles,
herein, we report the ﬁrst example of CuH-catalyzed C2
allylation of benzimidazoles with allenes ( Scheme 1 c).
The initial experiments were performed with N1-tethered
allene benzimidazole 1a−1c with the typical CuH catalytic
conditions (entries 1 −5o f Table 1). To our delight, Xantphos

was found to give the desired product 2b in a 54% yield, while
a byproduct 2b′ was obtained in a 16% yield (entry 4 of Table
1). Especially, the desired product 2c was obtained in an
excellent yield (entry 5 of Table 1). Subsequently, the reaction
of benzimidazole 1c was selected as the model reaction, and
the eﬀect of hydrosilane was investigated. Interestingly, the use
of 50 mol % of (MeO) 2MeSiH also gave the desired product
2c in an excellent yield (entry 7 of Table 1 ), which suggested
that this reaction perhaps followed a di ﬀerent catalytic
mechanism compared to a previous classic copper hydride
catalytic mechanism.
10,11 However, a further decrease of the
amount of (MeO) 2MeSiH decreased the yield signi ﬁcantly
(entries 8 and 9 of Table 1 ). Another commonly used
hydrosilane source, (EtO) 2MeSiH, was also checked. Unfortu-
nately, it only provided the desired product in a 61% yield
(entry 10 of Table 1). Further examination of various catalysts,
solvents, and ligands exhibited lower activity (see the
Supporting Information for details).
With the optimized reaction conditions in hand, we next
investigated the applicability of this cyclization protocol for
various benzimidazoles ( Scheme 2). The results demonstrated
that benzimidazoles bearing electron-donating, electron-with-
drawing, or electron-neutral groups were all well-tolerated in
this reaction, providing th e corresponding products in
moderate to excellent yields ( 2c−2q). Benzimidazoles bearing
a methyl substituent at di ﬀerent positions a ﬀorded the
corresponding products in 86 −96% yields ( 2d−2g). Good
yields were also obtained for other benzimidazoles containing
electron-donating groups, e.g., 5,6-dimethyl and 5-methoxy
(2h and 2i). Ester-containing substrate could provide the
desired product in a 90% yield ( 2j). Substrates containing
halogen groups (e.g., F, Cl, and Br) could also survive in this
CuH-catalyzed cyclization reaction, a ﬀording the correspond-
ing products in moderate to good yields ( 2k−2n). Other
substrates bearing electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., CF
3 and
CN) were also well-tolerated in this reaction ( 2o and 2p). A
good yield was also obtained for electron-neutral benzimida-
zoles (2q). However, N-containing heterocycles, imidazoles, or
triazoles tethered to allene could not provide the correspond-
ing products ( 2r−2t).
Encouraged by this cyclization protocol, we continued to
investigate the application of the copper hydride catalytic
system in the intermolecular C −H functionalization of
benzimidazoles with allenes. We continued our studies by
treatment of 1-methylbenzimidazole ( 3a) with cyclohexylal-
lene ( 4a) using the optimized reaction conditions of CuH-
catalyzed intramolecular C −H cyclization of benzimidazoles
with allenes ( Table 2 ). Fortunately, the desired product 5aa
was obtained in a moderate yield of 73% with 4:1 E/Z (entry 1
of Table 2 ). Subsequently, the e ﬀect of some other solvents
was examined. Notably, toluene as a solvent instead of
tetrahydrofuran (THF) led to a 93% yield with 15:1 E/Z

We next explored the scope of this allylation protocol by
examining various 1-methylbenzimidazoles ( Scheme 3 ). The
reaction proceeded e ﬃciently with 1-methylbenzimidazoles
bearing electron-donating and electron-withdrawing groups,
providing the corresponding products in moderate to good
yields with good E isomer selectivity ( 5aa−5ka). 1-
Methylbenzimidazoles bearing a methyl substituent at di ﬀerent
positions a ﬀorded the corresponding products in 69 −84%
yields with good E isomer selectivity ( 5ba−5ea). 1-
Methylbenzimidazoles containing a 5-methoxy group gave
the product in a moderate yield of 68% ( 5fa). Interestingly, an
ester-containing substrate could provide the desired product in
an 89% yield ( 5ga). Substrates containing halogen groups (e.g.,
F, Cl, and Br) a ﬀorded the corresponding products in
moderate yields ( 5ha−5ka). Unfortunately, Other substrates
bearing electron-withdrawing groups (e.g., CF
3 and CN) were
not suitable in this reaction ( 5la and 5ma). N-containing
heterocycles, imidazoles, or triazoles could not provide the
corresponding products ( 5na−5pa). Subsequently, we pro-
ceeded to explore the scope of allenes under the optimized
reaction conditions. Cyclohexylallene and cyclopentylallene
could provide the corresponding products in good yields ( 5aa
and 5ab). Phenylallene provided the desired product in a
moderate yield of 63% ( 5ac). Linear alkyl allenes were also
tolerated in this reaction, pr oviding the corresponding
products in moderate yields ( 5ad and 5ae). Unfortunately,
internal allene was unsuitable for this allylation protocol ( 5af).
To obtain further insight into this CuH-catalyzed C −H
allylation of benzimidazoles, some mechanistic experiments
were performed ( Scheme 4). Initially, C2-deuterated substrate
1c-d was reacted under the standard conditions of the
cyclization protocol (equation a). To our delight, signi ﬁcant
deuterium incorporation was observed at the alkene group of
compound 2c-d, which was di ﬀerent from the previous classic
copper hydride catalytic mechanism.
10,11 Subsequently, a
competition experiment between two di ﬀerent substrates
(1c-d and 1o) was performed under the standard conditions
of the cyclization protocol (equation b). Interestingly, two
deuterated products were observed. These results revealed that
there was a deuterium-scrambling distribution. Then, C2-
deuterated substrate 3a-d was reacted under the standard
conditions of the allylation protocol, and signi ﬁcant deuterium
incorporation was observed at the alkene group of 5aa-d
(equation c). A competition experiment between two di ﬀerent
substrates ( 3a-d and 3f) under the standard conditions of the
allylation protocol provided two deuterated products (equa-
tion d). These observations suggested that the hydrogen atom
at the C2 position of benzimidazoles could participate in the
formation of copper hydride species, which means that this
reaction follows a di ﬀerent catalytic mechanism compared to
the previous classic catalytic mechanism.
10,11
On the basis of the above results, a possible catalytic
mechanism for the cyclization protocol was proposed ( Scheme
5). The ﬁrst step would be the formation of LCuH species ( A)
with the assistance of (MeO) 2MeSiH and phosphine ligand.
The in situ generated LCuH species ( A) undergoes a
hydrocupration of allene 1c to generate allyl copper
intermediate B, which undergoes an intramolecular addition
to the C N bond to a ﬀord cyclization intermediate C. Then,
the interaction of this copper nitride intermediate C with the
hydrogen atom at the C2 position of benzimidazoles via a β-
hydride elimination regenerates the LCuH species ( A) to fulﬁll
the catalytic cycle and provides the desired product 2c (path
a). However, in mechanistic studies, the reaction of C2-
deuterated substrate 1c-d provided the product 2c-d in a 68%
deuterated ratio, which was 15% lower than substrate 1c-d.
This result suggested that there perhaps exists a secondary
catalytic cycle, which allows for generation of the intermediate

mechanism for the allylation protocol might follow a similar
mechanism as found for the cyclization protocol (see the
Supporting Information for details). The intermolecular
addition of compound 3a might undergo a process that
proceeds through a six-membered transition state A (TSA)i n
which the cyclohexyl group occupies the exocyclic axial
position, a ﬀording the E isomer intermediate C.T h e
corresponding transition state B (TSB)a ﬀording the minor
Z isomer intermediate C would require the cyclohexyl group to
occupy the endocyclic axial position, resulting in a steric
repulsion between the cyclohexyl group and benzimidazole,
which might explain the E isomer selectivity.
In conclusion, we have developed the ﬁrst example of
copper-hydride-catalyzed intra- and intermolecular C −H
functionalization of benzimidazoles with allenes, providing an
atom economy protocol for the synthesis of various
benzimidazole derivatives. In terms of green and sustainable
chemistry, the copper salt catalyst and mild reaction conditions
provide a particularly useful and energy-e ﬃcient tool for the
C−H functionalization of benzimidazoles. The new copper
hydride catalytic mechanism contributes more possibilities to
modern organic synthesis.
